strategy_title: Fix Hardcoded Grid to Respect Autotune XBLOCK
strategy_description: When a Triton kernel uses @triton.autotune with multiple XBLOCK configs but the caller computes the grid with a hardcoded constant (e.g., cdiv(xnumel, 128)) instead of meta['XBLOCK'], the grid size is always 1 regardless of which XBLOCK autotune selects, causing partial output and correctness failures. Changing the grid to a lambda `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)` allows autotune to correctly explore smaller XBLOCK values that spread work across more SMs. This reduced elapsed cycles from 3605 to 3249 (~10%) and warp cycles per issued instruction from 28.1 to 22.6, yielding a 1.11x speedup.
slow_pseudocode:
# Caller hardcodes XBLOCK in grid, ignoring autotune selection
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # always 1 block when xnumel=128
kernel[grid](args..., XBLOCK=128, R0_BLOCK=16)
fast_pseudocode:
# Grid lambda uses meta['XBLOCK'] so autotune can vary block count
grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
kernel[grid](args..., XBLOCK=128, R0_BLOCK=16)  # autotune picks best XBLOCK
applicable_when: Triton kernel has @triton.autotune with multiple XBLOCK configs, but the caller grid formula uses a hardcoded constant instead of meta['XBLOCK']. LaunchConfiguration NCU rule fires with high speedup_pct (>90%). Grid size is 1 while SM count is large (e.g., 132). Achieved occupancy is near 0% (1-2%) vs theoretical 50%+.
do_not_apply_when: Grid is already a lambda using meta['XBLOCK']. Kernel has no @triton.autotune or only one XBLOCK config. The workload is intentionally single-block (e.g., a global reduction where all threads must cooperate). Correctness requires all x-elements to be processed by a single program_id.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: the grid must be a Python lambda `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)` so that the autotuner can pass the selected XBLOCK via the meta dict. Using a static tuple for the grid bypasses autotune's block-size selection entirely. The kernel body needs xmask = xindex < xnumel guards on all loads/stores for this to be correct at any XBLOCK value.

strategy_title: Use Lambda Grid So Autotuner Controls Block Count
strategy_description: When a Triton kernel's grid is hardcoded as a static tuple (e.g., `(cdiv(N, XBLOCK_CONSTANT),)`), the autotuner can vary XBLOCK in the kernel configs but the grid size never changes, so all parallelism benefit is lost. Replacing the static grid with a lambda `lambda meta: (cdiv(N, meta['XBLOCK']),)` lets the grid adapt dynamically to whichever XBLOCK the autotuner selects, correctly distributing work across SMs. In this case the fix reduced elapsed cycles from 3605 to 3246 (10.5%) and warp cycles per issued instruction from 28.1 to 21.7, even though the workload is tiny (128 elements) and the kernel remains latency-bound.
slow_pseudocode:
# Static grid ignores autotuned XBLOCK — always launches 1 block
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # hardcoded XBLOCK=128 constant
my_kernel[grid](arg0, arg1, arg2, xnumel, r0_numel)
fast_pseudocode:
# Lambda grid adapts to autotuned XBLOCK — launches cdiv(N, XBLOCK) blocks
my_kernel[
    lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
](arg0, arg1, arg2, xnumel, r0_numel)
applicable_when: Triton kernel has @triton.autotune with multiple XBLOCK configs but the call-site grid is a static tuple using a hardcoded XBLOCK constant. LaunchConfiguration NCU rule fires with high speedup_pct (>90%). Grid size is 1 or very small relative to SM count. Achieved occupancy is far below theoretical occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: The kernel body does not have an xmask guard (partial tiles would be unsafe). The grid is already a lambda or the XBLOCK is not an autotuned parameter. The workload is large enough that a single block already saturates the SM.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: the grid argument to `kernel[grid](...)` can be a callable `lambda meta: (...)` where `meta` is the dict of autotuned config values. This is the standard Triton pattern for autotuned grids. In CUDA the equivalent is choosing launch bounds at runtime based on the tuned tile size.

strategy_description: When a Triton kernel shows L1/TEX throughput near or above 100% and CPIStall reports 40%+ of cycles stalled on L1TEX scoreboard waits, adding eviction_policy='evict_first' to streaming (non-reused) loads frees L1 cache lines for reused data, reducing cache pressure. Simultaneously, adding num_stages=2 to autotune configs enables Triton's software pipelining to overlap memory fetches with compute, hiding L1TEX latency. Together these changes reduced Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 28.1 to 22.6 (−20%) and L1/TEX throughput from 109% to 94%, yielding a ~10% wall-time reduction.
applicable_when: L1/TEX Cache Throughput >= 100%, CPIStall reports 40%+ of cycles stalled on L1TEX scoreboard dependency, kernel has a mix of streaming (single-use) and reused (e.g. bias) loads, and the kernel is small enough that software pipelining (num_stages=2) can hide memory latency without excessive register pressure.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is already register-pressure-limited (registers per thread near hardware max); num_stages=2 increases register usage and may reduce occupancy further. Also avoid evict_first if the data IS reused within the kernel (e.g., weights accessed multiple times per tile). Not applicable when L1/TEX throughput is low and the bottleneck is compute or DRAM bandwidth.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: num_stages in triton.Config controls software pipelining depth for the kernel's memory loads. eviction_policy='evict_first' and 'evict_last' are Triton load modifiers that map to PTX cache hints (.cs and .ca respectively). CUDA equivalent: __ldcs() for streaming, __ldca() for cached loads. num_stages has no direct CUDA equivalent — use __builtin_assume or manual prefetch loops instead.

strategy_title: Use Lambda Grid to Respect Autotuned XBLOCK in Triton
strategy_description: When a Triton kernel uses @triton.autotune with multiple XBLOCK configs but the launch site hardcodes the grid as `(cdiv(xnumel, FIXED_XBLOCK),)`, the grid size never adapts to the winning config, leaving most SMs idle. Replacing the hardcoded grid with `lambda meta: (cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)` allows the grid to scale with the autotuner's chosen XBLOCK. In this case the kernel was tiny (grid=1, 2.43 µs) so the improvement was modest (~7%), but the fix is structurally correct and prevents correctness failures that occurred in prior iterations when XBLOCK was reduced without updating the grid expression.
slow_pseudocode:
# BUG: grid hardcoded, ignores autotuned XBLOCK
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # always = 1
my_kernel[grid](arg_0, arg_1, arg_2, xnumel, r0_numel)
fast_pseudocode:
# FIX: grid adapts to whichever XBLOCK the autotuner selects
grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
my_kernel[grid](arg_0, arg_1, arg_2, xnumel, r0_numel)
applicable_when: A Triton kernel has @triton.autotune with multiple XBLOCK configs but the kernel_function launch site uses a hardcoded constant (e.g. cdiv(xnumel, 128)) instead of reading XBLOCK from meta. NCU LaunchConfiguration rule fires with high speedup_pct (>90%). Grid size is 1 or very small relative to SM count.
do_not_apply_when: The kernel does not use @triton.autotune, or the grid is already a lambda reading from meta['XBLOCK']. Also not applicable when the kernel body lacks an xmask guard (xindex < xnumel) — without the mask, non-power-of-two xnumel with small XBLOCK will cause out-of-bounds writes.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: the standard Inductor pattern for autotuned kernels is `grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)`. The meta dict is populated by the autotuner with the winning config's parameters. This is equivalent to CUDA's dynamic grid sizing based on chosen block dimensions.

strategy_title: Expanding num_stages in Autotune Configs for Tiny Kernels
strategy_description: Adding num_stages=2 variants to autotune configs for very small kernels (41 instructions, grid=1, ~2 µs) does not reliably improve performance and can cause regression. In this case, elapsed cycles increased from 3249 to 3435 (+5.7%) and Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction worsened from 22.6 to 28.9, despite the CPIStall rule suggesting L1TEX stalls as the bottleneck. The kernel is too small and fully unrolled (R0_BLOCK=16 compile-time constant) for software pipelining to provide meaningful latency hiding; the autotuner overhead and register pressure from num_stages=2 outweigh any benefit.
fast_pseudocode:
# After: 17 configs with num_stages in {1,2} and num_warps up to 16
# NOTE: this caused regression for this tiny kernel
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1},   num_warps=1,  num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1},   num_warps=1,  num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8,  num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=16, num_stages=2),
        # ...
    ],
    key=['xnumel', 'r0_numel'],
)
applicable_when: Kernel has a large loop body with many iterations, significant compute per load, and is NOT fully unrolled at compile time. CPIStall reports 40%+ of cycles stalled on L1TEX. Kernel duration is >10 µs with multiple waves across SMs.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is extremely small (<50 instructions, <3 µs, grid=1). The reduction dimension (R0_BLOCK) is a compile-time constant causing full loop unrolling — software pipelining cannot reorder already-unrolled instructions. Achieved occupancy is already near theoretical maximum. The kernel has no meaningful loop body for the pipeline to overlap.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: num_stages controls software pipeline depth for async memory prefetching. It is most effective when the kernel has a loop with multiple iterations that can be overlapped. For fully-unrolled kernels (small constexpr R0_BLOCK), num_stages=2 adds register pressure without providing latency hiding. The autotuner may select a num_stages=2 config that performs worse than the default num_stages=1.
